what_its_for: Nitroglycerin is used to treat and prevent chest pain (called angina). It works by relaxing and widening your blood vessels so your heart gets more blood and oxygen. Some forms are used when chest pain happens suddenly, while others are used regularly to help prevent chest pain from occurring.
how_to_take:
How you take nitroglycerin depends on the form your doctor prescribed: 

• SUBLINGUAL TABLET (under the tongue): At the first sign of chest pain, sit down and place 1 tablet under your tongue. Let it dissolve completely — do NOT swallow it, chew it, or crush it. If your chest pain does not go away after 5 minutes, take a second tablet. If pain still continues after another 5 minutes, take a third tablet. If pain is NOT relieved after 3 tablets (15 minutes total), call 911 immediately — this could be a heart attack. 

• SPRAY (Nitrolingual): Spray 1 or 2 sprays under your tongue or onto your tongue. Do NOT shake the can before using. Do NOT inhale the spray. Close your mouth after each spray. 

• PATCH (Nitro-Dur, Minitran): Apply the patch to clean, dry, hairless skin — good spots include your chest, upper arm, or back. Press firmly for 30 seconds. Change the patch location each time to avoid skin irritation. Remove the old patch before applying a new one. Most doctors recommend wearing the patch for 12–14 hours, then removing it for 10–12 hours (patch-free period) to keep it working well. 

• OINTMENT (Nitro-Bid): Use the special measuring paper provided to measure the correct amount. Spread the ointment in a thin, even layer on your skin (chest, back, or upper arm). Cover it with the measuring paper and tape it in place. Do NOT rub it in. Wear gloves or wash hands immediately after applying to avoid getting it on your hands.
dosing:
Your dose will depend on which form of nitroglycerin you are using and what your doctor prescribes. Typical dosing is: 

• Sublingual tablet: 0.3 mg, 0.4 mg, or 0.6 mg — 1 tablet as needed for chest pain (up to 3 tablets in 15 minutes). 

• Spray: 1 or 2 sprays (0.4 mg per spray) as needed (up to 3 sprays in 15 minutes). 

• Patch: 0.1 mg/hr to 0.8 mg/hr, worn 12–14 hours per day. 

• Ointment: Typically 1 to 2 inches applied every 6–8 hours. 

Always follow your doctor's specific instructions. Do not use more than directed.
missed_dose:
For the PATCH or OINTMENT (used on a schedule): If you forget to apply your patch or ointment, apply it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do NOT apply extra or double up to make up for a missed dose. 

For the TABLET or SPRAY (used only when you have chest pain): These are taken only when needed, so a 'missed dose' does not apply.
storage:
• TABLETS: Store in the original dark glass bottle with the lid tightly closed. Keep at room temperature (59°F to 77°F / 15°C to 25°C). Keep away from heat, light, and moisture. Do NOT store in the bathroom, near a stove, or in your car on hot days. Do NOT store in a pill organizer or transfer to a different container — this can make the tablets less effective. Replace your tablets every 6 months or by the expiration date on the bottle, whichever comes first. 

• SPRAY: Store at room temperature. Keep away from heat and open flames — the spray is flammable. Do NOT puncture or throw into a fire. 

• PATCH: Store at room temperature. Keep in original sealed pouch until ready to use. 

• OINTMENT: Store at room temperature with cap tightly closed. 

Keep ALL forms out of reach of children and pets.
what_to_avoid:
• ALCOHOL: Avoid drinking alcohol while using nitroglycerin. Combining them can cause a dangerous drop in blood pressure, dizziness, and fainting. 

• ERECTILE DYSFUNCTION (ED) MEDICATIONS: Do NOT take nitroglycerin if you have taken sildenafil (Viagra), tadalafil (Cialis), vardenafil (Levitra), or avanafil (Stendra) within the past 24–48 hours. This combination can cause a severe, life-threatening drop in blood pressure. Tell your doctor and emergency responders if you have taken any of these. 

• STANDING UP QUICKLY: Nitroglycerin can cause dizziness or lightheadedness, especially when you stand up fast. Sit or lie down when taking the sublingual tablet or spray to reduce the risk of fainting. 

• DRIVING AND OPERATING MACHINERY: Nitroglycerin can cause dizziness and headaches. Use caution until you know how this medication affects you. 

• HEAT and HOT ENVIRONMENTS: Avoid hot tubs, saunas, or prolonged hot showers when wearing the patch, as heat increases how much medication enters your body and may cause low blood pressure.
when_to_call_doctor:
Call your doctor if you experience: 
• Chest pain that is not relieved after 3 doses (tablets or sprays) in 15 minutes — CALL 911 FIRST, then your doctor 
• Severe headaches that do not improve over time (mild headaches are common at first and usually get better) 
• Dizziness, lightheadedness, or fainting 
• Fast or pounding heartbeat 
• Skin rash, redness, or irritation under the patch or from the ointment 
• Blurred vision 
• Nausea or vomiting that is severe or unusual 
• You feel your medication is not working as well as before 
• Any signs of a severe allergic reaction: rash, itching, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, or trouble breathing — call 911 immediately
when_it_works:
• SUBLINGUAL TABLET or SPRAY: These work very quickly — usually within 1 to 3 minutes — to relieve sudden chest pain. This is why they are used during an angina attack. 

• PATCH and OINTMENT: These work more slowly and are meant to prevent chest pain throughout the day. They are NOT for treating sudden chest pain. Always carry your fast-acting nitroglycerin (tablet or spray) with you for emergencies, even if you use a patch or ointment regularly.
special_populations:
• PREGNANCY: Talk to your doctor before using nitroglycerin if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Use only if your doctor decides the benefits outweigh the risks. 

• BREASTFEEDING: It is not known if nitroglycerin passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding while using this medication. 

• OLDER ADULTS (65+): Older adults may be more sensitive to the blood pressure-lowering effects of nitroglycerin and may have a higher risk of dizziness and falls. Sit or lie down when taking the tablet or spray, and stand up slowly. 

• KIDNEY or LIVER DISEASE: Let your doctor know if you have kidney or liver problems, as your dose may need to be adjusted. 

• ANEMIA or LOW BLOOD PRESSURE: If you have low blood pressure (hypotension) or certain types of anemia, nitroglycerin may not be safe for you. Make sure your doctor knows your full medical history.
